pages.x: Spain and Portugal had split the newly found world between them in 1494, and the spice-rich Moluccas lay somewhere on the far side. Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese captain serving Spain, promised the young King Charles to reach them by sailing west, around the Americas. In September 1519 five ships left Spain.

Among the crew was a young Italian scholar, Antonio Pigafetta, who paid his own way for the adventure. He wrote down everything: penguins and sea lions, giants he thought he saw in Patagonia, storms, and the words of the peoples they met. His diary is the reason we know the story.

In October 1520, after crushing a mutiny, the fleet found a maze of channels at the tip of South America, today the Strait of Magellan. One ship slipped away and sailed home. When the others came out into a calm ocean, Magellan named it the Pacific, the peaceful sea.

No one knew the Pacific was so wide. For more than three months they crossed it, eating biscuit dust, rats and leather softened in seawater. Scurvy swelled their gums until they could not eat at all, and 19 men died before they reached Guam.

In the Philippines Magellan won allies and converts, and promised to defeat a chief who refused to submit, Lapulapu of Mactan. On 27 April 1521 he waded ashore with about 50 men against some 1,500 warriors and was killed in the shallows. Filipinos honour Lapulapu as the first to resist Europe.

The survivors burned a ship they could no longer crew, reached the Moluccas and loaded cloves. Juan Sebastián Elcano took the Victoria home westward across the Indian Ocean and round Africa, keeping clear of the Portuguese, as men died of hunger on the way.

When the Victoria reached the Cape Verde Islands in July 1522, the crew found it was Thursday ashore, though their logs said Wednesday. Sailing west around the world, they had lost a day: the first sign of what the international date line deals with today.
On 6 September 1522 the Victoria limped into Sanlúcar with 18 Europeans aboard. Most of the others had died of scurvy, hunger, fighting and shipwreck, though a handful came home later.

The voyage proved that all the oceans are joined and showed how big the Earth really is. The cloves in the Victoria's hold paid for the whole expedition, and a Basque captain, not Magellan, completed the first circle of the world.
pts: Five ships sailed in 1519, one came back
Crossed the Pacific, far wider than anyone knew
Proved that the oceans are all joined
